label: US GDP Q2 2026 (Second Estimate)
source: BEA GDP Second Estimate, Q2 2026 (released August 26, 2026)
delta: Unrevised from advance estimate; down from Q1 2026's +2.1%
deltaNote: AUG 26 UPDATE — SECOND ESTIMATE CONFIRMS: Q2 2026 real GDP held at +1.5% annualized, unrevised from the July 30 advance estimate. An upward revision to consumer spending was offset by an upward revision to imports. Real GDI rose 2.2% (vs 1.2% in Q1); corporate profits rose $400.9B (vs $74.4B in Q1). The PCE price index within the report ran hot — 5.3% headline, 3.6% core — underscoring the stagflation-adjacent mix of sub-trend growth and above-target inflation heading into Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote (Aug 28). Prior: Q2 advance estimate (July 30): +1.5% annualized, missing the 2.1% consensus forecast; consumer spending +3.2%, net trade -1.0pp, inventories -0.7pp.

label: US Unemployment Rate
deltaNote: July 2026 (Aug 7): NFP fell 23,000 — a sharp miss vs the ~83,000 gain expected — with May and June revised down a combined 103,000. Unemployment eased to 4.1%, largely on lower labor-force participation rather than underlying strength. Markets read the report as reducing Fed hike risk; S&P 500 closed at a record high same day.

label: US PCE Inflation (May 2026 — Highest Since 2023)
deltaNote: MAY 2026 (released June 25): Headline PCE 4.1% YoY (+0.4% MoM) — highest since April 2023. Core PCE 3.4% YoY (vs 3.3% forecast). Personal income and spending each +0.7% MoM; saving rate held at 3%. Released just over a week after Warsh's hawkish dot plot, complicating the disinflation narrative even as Iran-deal oil relief began working through the data. June CPI (July 14) subsequently cooled to 3.5%, suggesting May PCE may mark the cycle high.

label: Fed Funds Rate
source: Federal Reserve FOMC, July 29 2026 (held; 3 hawkish dissents)
delta: Held at 3.50-3.75%; 3 dissents wanted a hike
deltaNote: July 28-29: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% despite the July 23 oil-driven inflation scare that had pushed September hike odds to ~82%. Three members dissented in favor of a hike — Warsh called it a 'good family fight.' The Aug 7 jobs miss (NFP -23K) subsequently cooled hike expectations for September. AUG 12-17 UPDATE: A Reuters poll of 104 economists found 94 expect the Fed to hold at 3.50-3.75% in September and 80 see no change through year-end; market pricing implies roughly 70% odds of a September hold, though futures still price in one hike by December. The Aug 17 expiration of the US-Iran MOU (no deal) and the resulting oil/yield jump added modest upside risk to hike bets even as the underlying data flow favors a hold.

label: ECB Deposit Facility Rate
source: ECB Governing Council, June 11 2026 (25bp hike — first since July 2023)
deltaNote: June 11: ECB raised all three key rates 25bp — deposit facility to 2.25%, main refi to 2.40%, marginal lending to 2.65% (effective June 17). First hike since July 2023, reversing the final step of the prior 8-cut easing cycle. New staff projections: HICP 3.0% (2026)/2.3% (2027)/2.0% (2028); growth cut to 0.8%/1.2%/1.5%. Lagarde left the door open to further tightening.

label: US 10Y / 30Y Treasury Yield
source: CNBC / Federal Reserve H.15 / FRED; July 23 - August 25, 2026
delta: Eased again: 10Y fell more than 7bps to 4.625% Aug 25 as markets looked past the Canada tariff escalation toward Nvidia earnings and Warsh's Aug 28 Jackson Hole keynote.
deltaNote: AUG 25 UPDATE: The 10-year Treasury yield fell over 7bps to 4.625% as a chip-sector rebound and easing near-term rate-hike bets outweighed the Canada retaliatory-tariff announcement. This continues the round-trip pattern since the Aug 17 peak: the 30-year hit 5.31-5.32% (highest since June 2007) when the US-Iran MOU expired without a deal, then eased through Aug 13's flat PPI before this latest pullback. National debt concerns (nearing $40T) and stubborn above-target inflation remain the structural floor under long-end yields even as near-term data (Aug 7 jobs miss, Aug 13 PPI) argues for a September Fed hold — a Reuters poll of 104 economists (Aug 12-17) found 94 expect a hold.

label: US Consumer Confidence (CB Index)
delta: +0.3 from Apr 2026 revised (beat 91.9 forecast; first monthly decline vs revised level)
deltaNote: May 2026: CB 93.1 (beat ~91.9 forecast; released May 26) — Present Situation Index 121.2 (down 3.2 pts); Expectations Index 74.4 (16th consecutive month below 80 recession-warning threshold). Two-thirds of consumers cutting spending due to inflation (highest proportion outside official recession). Michigan Final May 44.8 (all-time record low in 70+ year survey history).

label: Michigan Consumer Sentiment (August 2026 Preliminary)
deltaNote: AUG 2026 PRELIMINARY (released Aug 14): 51.0, badly missing the 54.5 consensus and down from July's final 55.2. Index of Consumer Expectations fell more sharply than Current Conditions; short-term expectations -11%, long-term projections -17%. Only 8% of consumers expect income growth to outpace inflation. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. Sentiment fell across demographic and political lines, sharpest among Republicans, older consumers, lower-income households, and those without college degrees. Still well above May 2026's all-time record low of 44.8, but the renewed slide — alongside July retail sales' steepest drop in over a year (Aug 14) — marks the clearest crack yet in the 'resilient consumer' narrative. Final August reading due Aug 28.

Markets recovered through Aug 25 (chip rebound, Canada tariff news shrugged off) and then broke to a fresh S&P 500 record Aug 27 on Nvidia's earnings beat ($96.2B revenue, +106% YoY) — the AI-capex narrative reasserting itself as the dominant growth-supportive story even as trade tensions with Canada escalate and the labor market softens. Attention now turns to incoming Fed Chair Warsh's Aug 28 Jackson Hole keynote, his first as Chair, with markets watching for any signal on the September 16-17 FOMC.

label: US Avg Effective Tariff Rate
value: Canada Section 338 Tariffs (50% on ~$20B) Took Effect Aug 22; Canada Retaliates With 15-50% Tariffs on $20B, Effective Sept 8
source: USTR / Global Trade Alert / Bloomberg / AP; July 24 - August 25, 2026
contestNote: US-Canada trade talks collapsed late Aug 21; the Section 338 tariffs (50% on ~$20B of Canadian autos, alcohol, and dairy) took effect Aug 22 (after a brief 3-day suspension from the original Aug 19 date). Carney declared Canada 'at war' with the US on trade. On Aug 25, Carney announced Canada's countermeasures: tiered 15%/25%/50% retaliatory tariffs on ~$20B of US goods across 700+ products (steel, aluminum, furniture, clothing at 50%; appliances, dairy, seafood at 25%; other industrial goods at 15%), effective September 8, plus a C$7.5B (US$5.4B) support package for affected workers and businesses. Two days later (Aug 24) Trump additionally threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, auto parts, and steel starting Jan 1, 2027. Separately, the Section 122/Section 301 transition (60 economies, 10-12.5%) that resolved July 24 remains in force; USMCA-qualifying goods stay exempt from Section 301.

Three July typhoons disrupted manufacturing hubs and fading subsidy support weighed on durable-goods spending. Beijing's late-July Politburo pledge of 'targeted stimulus' has yet to translate into major new measures.

label: Global Policy Uncertainty / Recession Risk
value: AUG 25: US-Canada Trade War Escalates (Retaliatory Tariffs Effective Sept 8); GDP Second Estimate + Jackson Hole + Nvidia Earnings All Land This Week
source: Federal Reserve / BEA / BLS / China NBS / Census Bureau / U. Michigan; July 17 – August 25, 2026
delta: AUG 19-25 ARC — TRADE WAR ESCALATES INTO A THREE-CATALYST WEEK: US-Canada talks collapsed Aug 21; Section 338 tariffs (50% on ~$20B of Canadian goods) took effect Aug 22 after a brief suspension; Carney declared Canada 'at war' with the US on trade. Trump escalated further Aug 24, threatening 50% tariffs on Canadian autos/steel from Jan 1, 2027. Canada announced its retaliatory tariffs Aug 25 (15-50% on ~$20B of US goods, effective Sept 8, plus a C$7.5B support package), though markets shrugged it off — the S&P 500 gained 0.3% and the 10Y yield eased 7bps to 4.625% as chip stocks rebounded ahead of Nvidia's earnings.
deltaNote: AUG 25 RECESSION RISK SNAPSHOT: Five distinct risk channels are now in play — a now-active US-Canada trade war (each side's tariffs escalating in real time), a bond market still structurally pressured by debt/inflation concerns even as it eases short-term, a deepening China slowdown, elevated equity valuations heading into Nvidia's Aug 26 report, and incoming Fed Chair Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote (Aug 28) — his clearest policy signal yet on whether 'no landing' becomes the Fed's operative framework. None individually rises to a 2026-recession-defining shock, but the density of catalysts in a single week (GDP second estimate + durable goods Aug 26, Nvidia earnings Aug 26, Jackson Hole Aug 27-29) raises the odds of a volatile turn. Next catalysts: Nvidia earnings (Aug 26 after close), Jackson Hole (Aug 27-29), final August Michigan sentiment (Aug 28), and the September 16-17 FOMC meeting.

label: BOJ Policy Rate
source: Bank of Japan, June 16 2026 (25bp hike — highest since 1995)
deltaNote: June 16: BOJ hiked 25bp to 1.00%, the highest level since 1995, in a 7-1 vote (Asada dissenting) — citing Iran-war energy-cost pass-through risk. The hike landed the same day Warsh's first FOMC opened, raising August-2024-style carry-unwind concerns; the immediate market reaction was orderly (Nikkei +0.46%), but the yen still fell to a fresh 40-year low past 162/USD by June 30 despite the hike and an estimated $72.5bn in prior FX intervention.
